Juvenile individuals of Arrhamphus sclerolepis, commonly known as the Southeastern snub-nosed garfish, exhibit a relatively slow growth trajectory compared to other beloniform fishes. Field surveys conducted in estuarine habitats of eastern Australia indicate that newly emerged yolk-sac larvae, having completed the trophic switch to exogenous feeding, initially weigh approximately 0.0042 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0042 grams]. This minute neonatal mass, derived from eggs with an average diameter of 2 millimeters, reflects a modest maternal investment per offspring. As these young fish progress through the juvenile stage, their growth in length follows a predictable pattern, and records from extensive gillnet sampling suggest that the ultimate total length attained by adults in this population is 28.0 centimeters [Li = 28.0 centimeters]. This asymptotic size is considerably smaller than that documented for the closely related congener Arrhamphus krefftii, a difference that may be linked to habitat-specific resource availability and thermal regimes. The rapid early growth phase is critically dependent upon successful first feeding and the subsequent accumulation of lipid reserves.

The onset of reproductive maturity in this species is closely tied to body size rather than chronological age per se, although extensive mark-recapture data provide a robust framework for estimating these life-history transitions. Gonadal inspection of captured individuals reveals that puberty is reliably achieved once a fish reaches a total length of 12 centimeters [Lp = 12 centimeters]. This threshold, which corresponds to individuals approximately one year of age, marks the initiation of gametogenesis and the capacity for participation in spawning events. The attainment of this length is a critical developmental milestone, after which resources can be directed toward reproductive effort. In contrast, first reproduction is typically deferred until a slightly larger size is reached, ensuring that females have accrued sufficient energy reserves to support the metabolic demands of oocyte development and spawning. The relatively small size at puberty compared to the ultimate total length implies a protracted adult phase during which multiple spawning events are possible across successive seasons.

Under controlled laboratory conditions designed to mimic the mean annual water temperature of the species' subtropical range, reproductive output has been quantified with precision. At a stable temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], females produce approximately 5 to 6 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 5 to 6 eggs per clutch] and typically complete approximately one spawning event per year [F_R_i = approximately one spawning event per year]. This annual reproductive allocation is notably low, a finding that aligns with the relatively high value of the somatic maintenance coefficient reported for this species and reflects the energetic constraints imposed by its elongated body plan. The eggs themselves, which are demersal and adhesive, are fertilized externally during synchronized spawning rushes near submerged aquatic vegetation. The incubation period lasts approximately 10 days at this temperature, after which the transparent, yolk-dependent embryos hatch. This modest fecundity per event, combined with infrequent spawning, results in a low overall reproductive rate compared to many other hemiramphid species that inhabit similar coastal environments.

Long-term monitoring of captive cohorts maintained at a constant water temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C] has provided valuable insights into the species' maximum longevity. The oldest documented individuals have been recorded living for 9 years [am = 9 years], a lifespan that is considerable for a fish of this modest maximum body size at a temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This extended adult phase, lasting approximately 8 years after the attainment of reproductive maturity, allows for repeat spawning over numerous seasons, potentially compensating for the low annual fecundity. The ultimate wet weight achieved by these longest-lived adults, as determined from periodic mass measurements, reaches 86 grams [Wwi = 86 grams], a value derived from the species-specific length-weight relationship. This asymptotic body mass is achieved gradually, with growth rates decelerating markedly after the fish surpass approximately 20 centimeters in total length. The observed longevity, combined with the slow growth and low reproductive output, positions this garfish as a relatively K-selected strategist among its coastal marine relatives.

Comparisons with other members of the family Hemiramphidae highlight the unique life-history profile of Arrhamphus sclerolepis. While many halfbeaks are characterized by rapid maturation and high fecundity, this species diverges markedly with its low annual reproductive rate, which is particularly constrained by the infrequent spawning events. The ultimate total length of 28.0 centimeters [Li = 28.0 centimeters] places it among the smaller members of the genus, yet its maximum lifespan of 9 years [am = 9 years] is among the longest recorded for any hemiramphid at a temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This extended lifespan, combined with the modest size at puberty of 12 centimeters [Lp = 12 centimeters], suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes survival and repeated reproductive bouts over a single, high-output spawning season. The relatively small wet weight at birth of 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams] necessitates a prolonged period of juvenile growth before the fish can successfully compete for resources and avoid predation. The ultimate wet weight of 86 grams [Wwi = 86 grams] further underscores the species' relatively diminutive adult body size.
